overview: Barramundi Limited is a NZX Main Board-listed closed-end investment company (inception 26 October 2006) that gives New Zealand investors a single, PIE-tax-efficient vehicle for a concentrated portfolio of growing Australian-listed (and occasionally unlisted) companies. Barramundi has no employees or operating business of its own: its board outsources all investment decisions to external manager Fisher Funds Management Limited, which applies a proprietary 'STEEPP' stock-selection process to build a ~25-35 stock portfolio of Australian mid/large-cap names (current top holdings include BHP Group, WiseTech Global, Macquarie Group, ANZ Group and AUB Group). It is not a growth compounder in the operating-company sense; it is a wrapper whose investor return equals the underlying Australian equity return, minus manager fees, plus or minus any change in the market's discount/premium to net asset value (NAV) — and FY2026 delivered a very poor outcome on both fronts.

business_model.summary: Barramundi earns no 'revenue' in the operating sense — its statement of comprehensive income comprises dividend and interest income from the portfolio (~$6-7m p.a.) plus (usually much larger and far more volatile) unrealised and realised gains/losses on the Australian equity portfolio and associated NZD/AUD currency hedges. FY2026 (year to 30-Jun-2026) delivered a net loss after tax of $42.9m, driven by a $46.0m loss on investments against $6.6m of dividend/interest/other income and $3.5m of operating expenses/fees/tax — a sharp deterioration from FY2025's $7.9m net profit. H1 FY2026 (six months to 31-Dec-2025) alone posted a $15.4m net loss as portfolio fair value fell $17.4m, before a further, larger deterioration in H2 FY2026. Barramundi is structured as a Portfolio Investment Entity (PIE) for NZ tax purposes, meaning most capital gains on ASX-listed holdings are tax-exempt to the company, and shareholders' distributions carry favourable PIE tax treatment relative to direct offshore share ownership.

revenue_streams.name: Dividend income from Australian equity portfolio
revenue_streams.trend: stable, modest (~2-3% yield on assets); this is the only genuinely recurring 'earnings' stream

revenue_streams.name: Net change in fair value of investments (capital gains/losses, realised + unrealised)
revenue_streams.trend: highly volatile and market-driven — FY2024 +$28.9m, FY2025 +$8.5m, H1 FY2026 -$17.4m, full FY2026 -$46.0m — this is the dominant, non-recurring swing factor in reported profit, not a business revenue stream

business_model.customer_type: NZ retail and wealth-adviser shareholders seeking diversified, PIE-tax-efficient exposure to Australian growth equities without direct ASX brokerage/FX/tax complexity; no institutional or wholesale 'customer' base in the operating-company sense
business_model.geographic_mix: 100% market risk concentrated in Australia (single operating segment: 'Australian financial investment'); reporting currency NZD but the large majority of assets are AUD-denominated Australian-listed equities, actively (but only partially) hedged back toward NZD via forward FX contracts at the Manager's discretion

main_competitors: Australian Foundation Investment Company (AFIC/AFI.NZ dual-listed peer LIC)
Marlin Global (Fisher Funds' sister international-equities LIC, also underperforming)
Fisher Funds' own open-ended Australian/international funds
ASX 200 / hedged Australian equity index ETFs available to NZ investors
Direct ASX share ownership via NZ brokers
competitive_position.market_position: Small-cap NZX-listed vehicle; shareholders' equity fell from $240.6m (1-Jul-2025) to well under $200m by 30-Jun-2026 after the $42.9m FY2026 loss and ongoing distributions/buybacks. NAV per share fell to roughly $0.53 by September 2026, with the share price trading at a persistent, wide discount (16-21% through September 2026, versus a 6% Board buyback-trigger threshold). Sub-scale relative to global peers, which caps secondary-market liquidity and limits the fund's ability to attract larger wholesale/KiwiSaver allocations.

moat_factors.description: As a Portfolio Investment Entity, most ASX capital gains are tax-exempt to Barramundi and distributions receive favourable PIE tax treatment for NZ resident shareholders versus direct offshore share ownership (typically subject to the Fair Dividend Rate regime) — a genuine structural advantage that is hard for a retail investor to replicate independently.

moat_factors.factor: Manager fee alignment / performance-fee downside protection
moat_factors.description: The base management fee mechanically steps down (0.1% per 1% of underperformance versus the NZ 90-Day Bank Bill Index, floor 0.75%) when the Manager underperforms — as it has for multiple consecutive quarters through FY2026 — partially cushioning shareholders during weak periods, unlike most externally managed funds where the base fee is fixed regardless of performance. No performance fee has been payable since FY2024.

Fisher Funds has managed the fund since 2006 using a documented 'STEEPP' process; but five consecutive quarters of material underperformance through FY2026, culminating in a -18.2% adjusted NAV return versus a +9.2% benchmark, has visibly strained this relationship — the Board disclosed 'extensive engagement' with the Manager regarding performance.

A ~25-35 stock concentrated portfolio theoretically allows genuine active-management alpha versus a passive index, but FY2025-FY2026 results show this concentration has been a persistent source of severe underperformance (technology/AI-related derating, classified-advertising and other stock-specific losses) rather than outperformance.

weaknesses: Severe and widening share price discount to NAV (16-21% through September 2026, versus the Board's 6% share-buyback trigger threshold) — the market has lost confidence that the vehicle converts NAV into shareholder value

Sustained, multi-quarter manager underperformance versus benchmark: FY2025 adjusted NAV return +3.9% vs benchmark +13.5%; H1 FY2026 -6.6% vs benchmark +5.6%; full FY2026 -18.2% vs benchmark +9.2% — one of the worst relative years in the fund's history, prompting explicit Board scrutiny of the Manager

8%-p.a. quarterly distribution policy (2% of average NAV per quarter) is materially higher than the portfolio's underlying dividend yield and, in a year of a large capital loss (FY2026), is entirely a return of shareholders' own capital, mechanically eroding the NAV base per share

Warrant issuance programme is a recurring, structurally dilutive feature: the Aug-2025 1-for-4 warrant tranche (BRMWI, final exercise price cut to $0.65 by 26-Jun-2026 from an original $0.70) still saw only 83,274 warrants exercised out of 85.2m issued by the 7-Aug-2026 expiry — almost the entire tranche lapsed worthless, denying the Company the expected capital raise and evidencing how far the share price/NAV had fallen versus the strike
Sub-scale fund size limits secondary-market liquidity, which can itself widen the discount in periods of selling pressure (a negative feedback loop)
Single-country, single-currency-block concentration (100% Australia) offers no diversification benefit versus a global or NZ-only alternative

Board and Chair turnover during a period of underperformance (Andy Coupe retired as Chair effective 30-Jun-2026, succeeded by Fiona Oliver; new director Simon Flood appointed 1-Jun-2026) adds governance transition risk at a sensitive time

growth_drivers: Potential discount narrowing: the Company operates an active share buyback programme triggered whenever the share price discount to last-published NAV exceeds 6% — at a 16-21% discount (September 2026), buybacks are strongly NAV-accretive per remaining share if executed at scale, and could be a mean-reversion catalyst

Portfolio pivot toward resources: additions of BHP Group and Rio Tinto since late 2025 (BHP now the single largest holding at ~7%) increase exposure to commodity price strength, diversifying away from the technology-heavy positioning that drove recent losses

Continued exposure to structural Australian/ASX growth and quality names (WiseTech, Macquarie Group, ANZ Group, AUB Group) offers participation in a recovery in technology, financials and insurance-broking sectors if the AI-driven derating proves temporary
Fee step-down mechanism (management fee cut toward the 0.75% floor amid sustained underperformance) partially self-corrects and creates a stronger incentive for the Manager to restore outperformance

Explicit Board engagement with Fisher Funds following the FY2026 loss could result in portfolio, process or (in an extreme scenario) manager changes that improve future outcomes, though this is speculative and unconfirmed
Dividend reinvestment plan (discount to VWAP) provides a modest structural NAV-accretion mechanic for participating shareholders

business.description: FY2026 adjusted NAV return of -18.2% versus benchmark +9.2% (a ~27 percentage point shortfall) followed FY2025's underperformance (+3.9% vs +13.5%) and H1 FY2026's (-6.6% vs +5.6%) — five consecutive quarters of weak relative results. The Board has disclosed 'extensive engagement' with Fisher Funds regarding performance, a material governance escalation.
A ~25-35 stock portfolio means individual company-specific shocks can meaningfully move NAV, as seen repeatedly through FY2025-FY2026 (technology and classified-advertising drawdowns).

Shareholders' equity fell well below $200m through FY2026 and thin secondary-market trading can amplify discount volatility, making it harder for larger investors to build or exit positions without moving the price.

Performance depends on Fisher Funds' portfolio team and the STEEPP process continuing to be applied effectively; sustained underperformance raises the live possibility of manager or process changes, which would itself be a transition risk for shareholders to underwrite.

financial.description: The large majority of assets are AUD-denominated Australian equities; NZ investors' NZD-denominated returns are exposed to AUD/NZD movements, and the Manager's variable forward FX hedging can itself add volatility rather than purely reduce it (H1 FY2026 saw a loss on forward FX contracts on top of the underlying equity loss).

financial.risk: Distribution exceeding earned return erodes capital
financial.description: The 8% p.a. (2% per quarter of average NAV) distribution policy is not tied to actual portfolio income or total return; FY2026's -18.2% NAV return means the ~5.25 cents/share paid during the year was entirely funded from a shrinking capital base, materially compounding the NAV per share decline.

financial.risk: Warrant dilution / overhang (in reverse: raise-shortfall risk)
financial.description: The Aug-2025 warrant tranche's near-total lapse (only 83,274 of 85.2m warrants exercised) shows the Company failed to realise its expected capital raise as NAV fell below the strike; future warrant issues remain a recurring capital-structure event, and successful ones would still dilute NAV if exercised below prevailing NAV per share.

regulatory.description: Barramundi's structural tax efficiency for NZ shareholders depends on continued PIE and imputation/FDR settings under NZ tax law; any adverse legislative change would reduce the vehicle's relative attractiveness.

As an FMC Reporting Entity under the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 and NZX Main Board listed issuer, Barramundi bears ongoing compliance, audit, custody, and climate-reporting costs that scale poorly for a sub-scale, shrinking fund.

macro.description: As a heavily invested Australian equity vehicle, NAV moves largely one-for-one (before currency and stock-selection effects) with the ASX, making the stock highly cyclical and directly exposed to any Australian or global equity market downturn — though FY2026's loss occurred despite the benchmark itself rising +9.2%, underscoring that stock selection, not the market, was the dominant driver.

FY2025-FY2026 underperformance was repeatedly attributed in part to AI-related investor concerns hitting information technology holdings; continued volatility in AI-driven technology valuations is a live risk given the portfolio's technology weighting (WiseTech and others).
The now-larger BHP Group position (top holding, ~7% of portfolio) and Rio Tinto increase sensitivity to iron ore and broader commodity price cycles.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Australian equities (S&P/ASX 200) rose through FY2026 (benchmark +9.2% for the year to Jun-2026), so Barramundi's severe underperformance is a manager/stock-selection issue rather than a reflection of a weak Australian equity backdrop — the fund's fortunes currently hinge on whether Fisher Funds can arrest a multi-quarter run of poor relative results.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High — as a heavily invested single-country equity closed-end fund, both NAV and the traded share price (further amplified by discount/premium swings) are directly cyclical with the Australian sharemarket and the AUD/NZD exchange rate.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Low direct sensitivity (no company borrowings currently outstanding, no bond-like liabilities), but the NZ 90-Day Bank Bill Index sets both the management-fee reduction threshold and the performance-fee hurdle (Bank Bill Index + 7%), so relative NZ interest-rate levels affect the fee economics between Barramundi and Fisher Funds.
key_input_costs: Management fees paid to Fisher Funds (1.25% of gross asset value, stepping down to a 0.75% floor on sustained underperformance — near or at the floor through FY2026)
Potential performance fees (10% of excess return over the hurdle, capped at 1.25% of adjusted NAV, subject to high-water mark; none paid since FY2024)
Custody, audit, NZX and administration costs

recent_developments.event: Discount to NAV widened further and remains extreme: NAV $0.5301 (16-Sep-2026) and $0.5348 (23-Sep-2026) against a share price of $0.45, an approximately 16-21% discount, well above the 6% buyback trigger; the Company continues to hold treasury stock (2.32m shares) acquired under the ongoing buyback programme.

FY2026 annual result (year to 30-Jun-2026): net loss after tax of $42.9m (loss on investments $46.0m, dividend/interest/other income $6.6m, less $3.5m expenses/fees/tax). Adjusted NAV return of -18.2% (gross -17.0%) versus the benchmark's +9.2% — one of the worst relative years on record. New Chair Fiona Oliver stated the result was 'very disappointing' and that 'the Board is acutely aware that this result is not satisfactory to shareholders and is working closely with the Manager to address the situation.' Board declared a further dividend of 1.07 cents/share (record date 3-Sep-2026, paid 25-Sep-2026); total distributions for the year were 5.25 cents/share.

BRMWI warrant tranche (issued Aug-2025, 85.2m warrants) expired with only 83,274 warrants exercised at the reduced final exercise price of $0.65 — the vast majority lapsed unexercised as the share price/NAV remained well below the strike, denying the Company its expected capital raise.
Final exercise price of the BRMWI warrants reset down to $0.65 (from an original $0.70) ahead of the 7-Aug-2026 exercise date, reflecting the declining NAV/share price.

Board renewal: Simon Flood appointed independent director effective 1-Jun-2026; Chair Andy Coupe retired effective 30-Jun-2026, succeeded by Fiona Oliver (independent director since Jun-2022) — a leadership transition occurring in the midst of the fund's worst relative-performance year.

H1 FY2026 interim result (six months to 31-Dec-2025): net loss after tax of $15.4m (vs $8.9m profit pcp); adjusted NAV return -6.6% vs benchmark +5.6%. Then-Chair Andy Coupe acknowledged 'a tough period' driven by weak technology and classified-advertising holdings amid AI-related investor concerns; management fee stepped down from 1.25% to 0.75% of gross asset value due to underperformance versus the Bank Bill Index.

Manager added BHP Group and Rio Tinto to the portfolio to capture commodity price strength, a shift away from the fund's traditional technology/healthcare/financials tilt; by Sep-2026, BHP had become the single largest holding (~7% of the portfolio), ahead of WiseTech, Macquarie Group, ANZ Group and AUB Group.

items.target: 2% of average NAV per quarter (~8% p.a.)
items.notes: Standing Board policy, not tied to actual earned NAV return. Given FY2026's -18.2% adjusted NAV return, the full 5.25 cents/share paid during the year was a return of shareholder capital; a further 1.07 cents/share was declared 24-Aug-2026, paid 25-Sep-2026.

items.target: Buybacks activated whenever the discount to last-published NAV exceeds 6% (up to 5% of shares on issue in any 12-month period)
items.notes: Discount has remained far above threshold through September 2026 (16-21%); the Company continues to accumulate treasury stock under the programme.

items.target: 1.25% of gross asset value p.a., reducible to a 0.75% floor for underperformance versus the NZ 90-Day Bank Bill Index (0.1% reduction per 1% of underperformance)
items.notes: Fee likely at or near the 0.75% floor through FY2026 given the scale of underperformance versus the Bank Bill Index.

items.target: 10% (plus GST) of excess return above the Bank Bill Index + 7% hurdle, capped at 1.25% of adjusted NAV, subject to a high-water mark
items.notes: No performance fee earned in FY2025 or FY2026 given the NAV return has been well below the hurdle/high-water mark in both years.

guidance.management_commentary: Chair Fiona Oliver (24-Aug-2026, on the FY2026 result): 'Barramundi has reported a very disappointing loss in what has been a volatile year for global share markets. The Board is acutely aware that this result is not satisfactory to shareholders and is working closely with the Manager to address the situation.' This follows former Chair Andy Coupe's Feb-2026 comment describing H1 FY2026 as 'a tough period' driven by technology and classified-advertising weakness amid AI-related investor concerns, and FY2025 commentary describing that year's result as 'disappointing' despite global market strength. The consistent multi-period tone of disappointment, combined with explicit Board-Manager engagement disclosed in FY2026, signals rising governance pressure on Fisher Funds to demonstrate a credible path back to benchmark-competitive performance.

bull_case: The discount to NAV has widened to an unusually extreme 16-21% by September 2026, well beyond the 6% buyback trigger — active, funded buybacks at this discount are directly and significantly NAV-accretive for remaining shareholders and a potential mean-reversion catalyst if sentiment or performance improves

PIE tax-efficient structure gives NZ investors simplified, favourably taxed exposure to a diversified basket of Australian companies (BHP, WiseTech, Macquarie, ANZ, AUB) without direct ASX brokerage, FX conversion or FIF/FDR tax complexity
The manager fee reduction mechanism (1.25% down to a 0.75% floor during underperformance) partially self-corrects and reduces the fee drag precisely when performance is weakest

Explicit Board scrutiny and 'extensive engagement' with Fisher Funds following the FY2026 loss, plus new Board leadership (Chair Fiona Oliver, director Simon Flood), could catalyse portfolio, process, or even manager changes that improve future risk-adjusted returns

A buyer today is effectively acquiring a diversified, liquid, ASX-listed equity portfolio at a large discount to its stated NAV, with optionality on both a discount-narrowing catalyst and a recovery in beaten-down technology/quality holdings
bear_case: FY2026 delivered a -18.2% adjusted NAV return against a benchmark that rose +9.2% — one of the worst relative years in the fund's history — following two prior periods of underperformance (FY2025, H1 FY2026); this is not a one-off shock but a sustained, five-consecutive-quarter pattern that calls into question the Manager's current process and stock selection

The 8% p.a. distribution policy is not organic income (portfolio dividend yield is a fraction of that) — in a year of an 18% capital loss, the entire distribution paid was a return of shareholders' own capital, compounding the NAV per share decline rather than reflecting real earnings

The share price discount to NAV has continued to widen even as the Board activates buybacks (16-21% through September 2026, up from 11-13% in July), suggesting the market has structurally lost confidence in the vehicle and that buybacks alone are insufficient to arrest the trend

The Aug-2025 warrant tranche's near-total failure to exercise (83,274 of 85.2m warrants) demonstrates how far the share price has fallen and signals continued investor reluctance to commit fresh capital to the fund even at a reduced strike price

Governance is in transition (new Chair, new director) at the exact moment performance is at its weakest, adding execution/transition risk on top of the sub-scale size, single-country concentration, and structural fee drag that a low-cost hedged ASX 200 ETF alternative does not carry
